main.title: id Software
main.subtitle: The Small Studio That Turned the PC Into a Machine for Speed
main.summary: On February 1, 1991, John Carmack, John Romero and Adrian Carmack leave Softdisk and give formal shape to id Software; Tom Hall completes his transition shortly afterward while continuing to contribute to the group.

cards.heading: The Small Studio That Turned the PC Into a Machine for Speed
cards.text: John Carmack, John Romero and Adrian Carmack left Softdisk to establish id Software on February 1, 1991. Tom Hall completed his transition shortly afterwards while continuing to contribute. Commander Keen had demonstrated the group's smooth PC scrolling; Wolfenstein 3D, Doom and Quake would develop its fast action, engine technology and multiplayer work. Shareware and tools for user-made content helped those games reach communities beyond their original releases.

cards.heading: Leaving the Office With an Engine in Mind
cards.text: The group began working in Shreveport after months of rapid game production for Softdisk's Gamer's Edge. Tight deadlines encouraged reusable tools, while Commander Keen supplied a demonstrated scrolling technique and a successful game. Tom Hall continued contributing after work while arranging his departure. The new company brought together experience already gained through building and distributing those projects.

cards.heading: A Free First Episode Changes Distribution
cards.text: Apogee founder Scott Miller distributed Commander Keen's first episode as shareware and sold the remaining episodes. Bulletin boards, copies between friends and software collections carried the free file before the Web became widespread. Players could try the game first and pay to continue. id later used the same approach with Wolfenstein 3D and Doom.

cards.heading: Doom Turns the Level Into a Shared Language
cards.text: Doom separated important game data from its engine, making user-created levels and modifications practical through WAD files. Networked deathmatch let players compete directly, while shared files extended the game beyond id's original maps. Communities could study, change and distribute new spaces using the game's rules and technology.

main.title: Metal Storm
main.subtitle: Turn the room upside down
main.summary: Metal Storm is an NES action platformer built around the M-308 Gunner, a robot capable of reversing gravity. The player can transfer from floor to ceiling, changing which surface provides safety and which direction an obstacle must be approached from. Tamtex makes that ability the foundation of the entire game rather than a temporary novelty. Shooting remains important, but understanding a room’s two orientations is the essential skill. A corridor can contain another route simply because the player chooses to treat its ceiling as the ground.

cards.heading: Turn the room upside down
cards.text: Metal Storm is an NES action platformer built around the M-308 Gunner, a robot capable of reversing gravity. The player can transfer from floor to ceiling, changing which surface provides safety and which direction an obstacle must be approached from. Tamtex makes that ability the foundation of the entire game rather than a temporary novelty. Shooting remains important, but understanding a room’s two orientations is the essential skill. A corridor can contain another route simply because the player chooses to treat its ceiling as the ground.

cards.heading: One switch, several consequences
cards.text: Reversing gravity changes the robot’s position relative to projectiles, barriers and machinery. Some hazards behave differently according to its orientation, so a switch can solve one problem while exposing another. Later stages add screen-wrapping, allowing an exit from one edge to become an entrance from the opposite side. The player must keep track of those relationships while moving and firing. Metal Storm asks for spatial understanding through a very small number of actions, letting the level arrangement supply most of the complexity.

cards.heading: Learning a second arrangement
cards.text: The available power-ups include a stronger beam, a shield and protection during a gravity change, but only one can be held at a time. Movement and positioning consequently remain important even when a useful item has been collected. Completing the game unlocks an Expert Mode that rearranges enemies and hazards and changes boss patterns. Familiar rooms become new problems rather than merely faster repetitions. It is an extension of the original idea: understanding where the robot can stand matters as much as recognising the room it occupies.

main.title: Blizzard Entertainment
main.subtitle: From Three Graduates to Worlds Lived In for Decades
main.summary: On February 8, 1991, Allen Adham, Michael Morhaime and Frank Pearce found Silicon & Synapse.

cards.heading: From Three Graduates to Worlds Lived In for Decades
cards.text: Allen Adham, Michael Morhaime and Frank Pearce founded Silicon & Synapse on February 8, 1991. The studio that became Blizzard began with ports and smaller projects before building Warcraft, Diablo and StarCraft. Battle.net connected players through a shared online service, and World of Warcraft later expanded the company's work in persistent online worlds.

cards.heading: Three Graduates Learn the Craft Through Ports
cards.text: Silicon & Synapse's early projects included moving games between platforms. Each port required adapting existing code, controls and graphics to different memory and hardware limits. These commissions preceded the studio's major original franchises and supplied practical experience for the team as it grew.

cards.heading: Warcraft Turns Strategy into a Serialized World
cards.text: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans arrived in 1994 with separate Human and Orc campaigns. Resource gathering, base construction and unit production supported real-time battles between recognisable factions. Their voices, buildings and roles gave the strategy a particular setting. Multiplayer extended those battles beyond the authored campaigns, while later releases continued the world's story.

cards.heading: Battle.net Moves the Center from Disc to Network
cards.text: Diablo introduced Battle.net as part of Blizzard's games in 1996. Chat, player discovery and creating games made it easier for owners to find people to play with. The shared service continued to develop alongside subsequent releases. Maintaining online play also meant responding to the communities, problems and habits visible through the network.

main.title: Lemmings
main.summary: Lemmings is a 1991 puzzle and strategy video game developed by DMA Design and published by Psygnosis for the Amiga.

cards.heading: DMA Design and the Amiga original
cards.text: Lemmings is a 1991 puzzle and strategy video game developed by DMA Design and published by Psygnosis for the Amiga. It was later ported to numerous other platforms. The game was programmed by Russell Kay, Mike Dailly and David Jones, and was inspired by a simple animation that Dailly created while experimenting with Deluxe Paint.

cards.heading: Eight skills to reach the exit
cards.text: The objective of the game is to guide a group of anthropomorphised lemmings through a number of obstacles to a designated exit. In any given level, the player must save a specified number or percentage of the lemmings in order to advance. To this end, the player must decide how to assign limited quantities of eight different skills to individual lemmings, allowing them to alter the landscape and/or their own behaviour so that enough of the lemmings can reach the exit safely.

cards.heading: Reception and the many ports
cards.text: Lemmings was one of the best-received video games of the early 1990s. It was the second-highest-rated game in the history of Amstrad Action, and was considered the eighth-greatest game of all time by Next Generation in 1996. Lemmings is also one of the most widely ported video games, and is estimated to have sold around 20 million copies between its various ports. The popularity of the game also led to the creation of several other Lemmings games, remakes and spin-offs, and has also inspired similar games. However, Lemmings lost considerable popularity by the late 1990s, which was attributed in part to its slow pace of gameplay compared to games of later generations.

main.title: Power Blade
main.subtitle: Natsume / Taito · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Power Blade is an NES action platformer published by Taito, following NOVA through a futuristic computer system seized by aliens. Six sectors hold data tapes needed to reach the central control area. NOVA's weapon is an energy boomerang that can be thrown in eight directions, giving the player useful angles against threats above and below. The mission combines jumping and combat with a search inside each sector. Reaching its end requires finding the person who can provide access to the protected database.

cards.heading: A boomerang against the computer takeover
cards.text: Power Blade is an NES action platformer published by Taito, following NOVA through a futuristic computer system seized by aliens. Six sectors hold data tapes needed to reach the central control area. NOVA's weapon is an energy boomerang that can be thrown in eight directions, giving the player useful angles against threats above and below. The mission combines jumping and combat with a search inside each sector. Reaching its end requires finding the person who can provide access to the protected database.

cards.heading: Find the agent before the security room
cards.text: The six sectors can be tackled in a chosen order. Within each one, an agent supplies an identification card that opens the way toward its security room and boss. Collecting the tape after that encounter brings the central objective closer. Power-ups improve the boomerang's range, strength and number of projectiles, while a power suit adds another means of surviving the opposition. The stage becomes a small assignment with several connected tasks, rather than simply a stretch of hazards leading to an exit.

cards.heading: A localisation that rebuilt the action
cards.text: Power Blade substantially reworked the earlier Japanese game Power Blazer. Levels, the hero's appearance and the controls changed, while the agents and multidirectional weapon gave the overseas release a different rhythm. Its North American debut followed in 1991, with a European edition in 1992. Kinuyo Yamashita composed the score, and Mike Winterbauer created the muscular cover illustration. The changes make this an unusually substantial example of localisation: the journey from one region to another also produced a different approach to moving and fighting through a stage.

main.title: Street Fighter II
main.subtitle: A conversation in six buttons
main.summary: Capcom's fighting game made differences between characters the foundation of competitive play.

cards.heading: Learning a character and an opponent
cards.text: Capcom's Street Fighter II is an arcade fighting game built around a varied cast with different reach, movement and special attacks. Learning a character means practising those particular tools. Against another person, success also requires adapting to how the opponent uses a different set of moves.

cards.heading: A culture built around the cabinet
cards.text: Its competition depended on meeting places, repeated encounters and the exchange of techniques. The sound and music of composers including Yoko Shimomura helped give each contest a place and a memorable identity.

features.title: Yoko Shimomura: hearing the loop
features.summary: Repetition changes the work of composing.

cards.heading: An imagined musical map
cards.text: Shimomura recalled a planner asking for character themes for Street Fighter II. She proposed using imagined impressions of their countries instead, matching the game's exaggerated scenery. The resulting music reflected that playful interpretation rather than an attempt to reproduce each country's traditions. A discussion about the stages gave the soundtrack its direction.

cards.heading: Writing for another return
cards.text: A loop asks something of the listener each time it returns. Shimomura contrasted a brief arcade encounter with hours spent inside an RPG. While writing, she listened for passages that became tiring through repetition and reduced an overemphatic phrase when necessary. Her test was not simply whether a tune attracted attention once. It was whether it continued to occupy the same space comfortably. That distinction makes restraint part of composition: an elaborate moment can become less useful when the game keeps asking it to return.

cards.heading: Other hands shape the concert
cards.text: For Symphonic Fantasies in 2009, Shimomura praised Jonne Valtonen's arrangement of Kingdom Hearts and Benyamin Nuss's demanding piano performance. She welcomed hearing the music reshaped for a concert. The arrangement and performance brought familiar melodies into a different form, with choices made by musicians beyond their original composer.

cards.heading: An album begins with requests
cards.text: Requests from listeners helped encourage Kingdom Hearts Piano Collections. Shimomura recalled fan emails, existing piano arrangements and support from Square Enix's music producers. These interests came together in an album devoted to the instrument. Music first written for a game acquired another setting through audience demand and production support.

cards.heading: An online conversation finds a venue
cards.text: Evo's own history begins in Northern California. In 1996, Tony Cannon and Tom Cannon worked with online Street Fighter communities to gather players at Sunnyvale Golfland for Battle by the Bay. Super Street Fighter II Turbo and Street Fighter Alpha 2 supplied two different contests. The account remembers Alex Valle defeating John Choi in the Alpha 2 final. Before the event could have a famous result, somebody had to connect the people discussing these games with a place where they could actually meet and play.

cards.heading: The meeting changes its name
cards.text: Later meetings moved to Folsom and then to UCLA in 2002 under the Evolution name. The 2001 tournament included Japanese competitors alongside American players, with different champions across its games. Keeping the event going involved changing venues, software and participants while preserving a place for those contests to happen.

cards.heading: From helping out to running pools
cards.text: Andrés Velasco y Coll describes another route into that work. He hosted tournaments at Florida International University, later met Evo organiser Albert Carmona, and offered technical help at Carmona's home arcade. Judging pools and updating brackets followed. Looking back on Evo 2016, he explains that his responsibilities included assembling a team, training judges, making schedules and handling disputes. This was work participants might notice mainly when it failed. A competitive match needed people to know where to go, whose turn came next and which rules applied.

cards.heading: A schedule has consequences
cards.text: Velasco y Coll acknowledged insufficient planning behind delayed Mortal Kombat X semifinals at Evo 2016. He described paper-bracket updates overwhelming the people processing them and argued for digital tools. More competitors increased the information, equipment and scheduling work needed between matches, making those systems important to keeping the tournament running.

main.title: Golden Axe Warrior
main.subtitle: Death Adder’s world to explore
main.summary: Golden Axe Warrior is Sega's overhead action adventure, first released for Master System in North America in April 1991.

cards.heading: Death Adder’s world to explore
cards.text: Golden Axe Warrior is Sega's overhead action adventure, first released for Master System in North America in April 1991. A young warrior crosses Firewood and its neighbouring lands to recover nine crystals and confront Death Adder. The familiar enemy connects it to Golden Axe, while towns, hidden labyrinths and an explorable overworld give the journey a different structure. Direct fighting takes place inside those spaces, with collected equipment and learned magic steadily expanding the hero's options. Reaching the tyrant depends on finding what his conquest has scattered across the world.

cards.heading: Finding the hidden labyrinth
cards.text: Each crystal is held in a labyrinth containing enemies, puzzles and a guarding boss. Locating those places is part of the task, with more than two hundred overworld screens providing a landscape to search. Towns offer equipment and supplies bought with horns gathered from enemies. Improved weapons and armour strengthen the warrior, while magical abilities consume a limited stock of pots. The journey therefore moves between discovery and preparation, as the next hidden passage may ask for an item or enough resources to survive the dungeon beyond it.

cards.heading: A tool opens the landscape
cards.text: An axe can cut down trees, while Earth magic clears rocks, allowing ordinary scenery to conceal another route. Acquiring those tools changes what the player can investigate in places already visited. Gathering the nine crystals eventually opens the final labyrinth, where the Golden Axe itself becomes essential to confronting Death Adder. Chikako Kamatani composed the music. The adventure's appeal lies in the changing relationship with its map: a screen that once seemed closed can reveal another purpose after the warrior returns with the ability to alter it.

main.title: Cave Noire
main.subtitle: Konami · Game Boy
main.summary: Cave Noire is Konami's Game Boy dungeon game about a new adventurer seeking a place in the guild of Karuzu. Four kinds of quest ask the player to defeat monsters, rescue fairies or collect a required amount of treasure. Each attempt creates another dungeon, making the destination a practical target rather than a fixed story route. The player has one chance to complete the assignment. A failed expedition leads to another layout, while success opens a harder version of the same kind of task.

cards.heading: A short expedition with one clear objective
cards.text: Cave Noire is Konami's Game Boy dungeon game about a new adventurer seeking a place in the guild of Karuzu. Four kinds of quest ask the player to defeat monsters, rescue fairies or collect a required amount of treasure. Each attempt creates another dungeon, making the destination a practical target rather than a fixed story route. The player has one chance to complete the assignment. A failed expedition leads to another layout, while success opens a harder version of the same kind of task.

cards.heading: An enemy moves when the adventurer does
cards.text: Movement and combat proceed in turns, giving the player time to consider a position before committing to it. Adjacent opponents can exchange attacks, while items change the chances of surviving a dangerous room. A potion, spell or piece of equipment may provide a safer alternative to fighting every creature directly. The objective matters because clearing the whole dungeon is not always necessary. A successful expedition can depend on recognising when enough has been accomplished and choosing a route that avoids an unnecessary final risk.

cards.heading: The game saves the achievement, not the expedition
cards.text: Ten difficulty levels develop each quest type, with successful completions recorded between sessions. Equipment and the changing dungeon belong to the current attempt rather than a permanent character carried unchanged through every journey. Released only in Japan in 1991, Cave Noire gives the portable format a concise version of the roguelike idea. Its individual expeditions are small enough to approach as a single problem, while the saved ladder of harder assignments supplies a longer reason to return and apply what the last attempt taught.

main.title: The G.G. Shinobi
main.subtitle: Joe Musashi needs his allies
main.summary: The G.G. Shinobi is Sega's ninja platform adventure, first released for Game Gear in Japan on 26 April 1991.

cards.heading: Joe Musashi needs his allies
cards.text: The G.G. Shinobi is Sega's ninja platform adventure, first released for Game Gear in Japan on 26 April 1991. Joe Musashi enters Neo City to rescue four captured comrades and stop the power threatening Ninja Valley. Each rescued ninja becomes playable, bringing a different weapon, movement ability and magical technique into the group. The portable game therefore gives the familiar sword-fighting journey a growing cast with practical uses. Progress means recovering the people whose skills will eventually allow the whole team to cross the enemy's most dangerous rooms.

cards.heading: Choosing the first rescue
cards.text: The first four stages can be attempted in any order. Choosing which comrade to rescue first determines which additional abilities become available for the remaining locations. Each character's different equipment and movement changes the immediate approach to enemies and obstacles. Joe begins the mission alone, but successful rescues turn the campaign into a collection of possible responses. A route that is awkward with one ninja can become more manageable with another, giving the player a reason to think about the sequence of stages as well as the action within them.

cards.heading: Five ninjas for the final fortress
cards.text: After the four rescues, Neo City becomes a network of trap rooms that require particular ninjas to cross. Many rooms offer two exits into further challenges, testing the combined abilities gathered during the earlier missions. The final area makes the rescue structure pay off directly: each companion is needed because of what that character can do. Yuzo Koshiro composed the soundtrack. The small handheld adventure gains its scale from the team, with five distinct skill sets turning a compact selection of stages into a connected problem of route, ability and timing.

main.title: Lagrange Point
main.subtitle: Konami · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Lagrange Point is Konami's science-fiction role-playing game for the Famicom, set among artificial space colonies. A biological disaster cuts off communication with Land-2, and a research expedition arrives to investigate. Its pilot Gene survives an attack and begins searching for the people who might explain what happened. The setting replaces a familiar fantasy kingdom with settlements built to sustain human life away from Earth. Moving between their inhabitants and dangerous surroundings gives the emergency a human scale before the larger conflict becomes clear.

cards.heading: A disaster beyond Earth
cards.text: Lagrange Point is Konami's science-fiction role-playing game for the Famicom, set among artificial space colonies. A biological disaster cuts off communication with Land-2, and a research expedition arrives to investigate. Its pilot Gene survives an attack and begins searching for the people who might explain what happened. The setting replaces a familiar fantasy kingdom with settlements built to sustain human life away from Earth. Moving between their inhabitants and dangerous surroundings gives the emergency a human scale before the larger conflict becomes clear.

cards.heading: Follow the surviving accounts
cards.text: The Isis Cluster contains two artificial biospheres and a satellite, placing the journey within a connected human settlement rather than an unexplored distant planet. Gene's damaged expedition leaves him dependent on the people and information found after his arrival. The search for a researcher from the Bio Research Lab gives the early investigation a concrete destination. The game uses a role-playing adventure's gradual discovery of places and companions to reveal how a planned new home has become a place threatened by its own catastrophe.

cards.heading: A cartridge with another musical voice
cards.text: Konami placed its VRC7 chip inside the cartridge, giving the music FM synthesis capabilities beyond the Famicom's ordinary sound hardware. That makes the soundtrack an important part of the game's technological identity as well as its atmosphere. The original release remained in Japan; an unofficial English translation followed in 2014. Its title refers to positions in space where the relationship between two large bodies can keep a third in a stable configuration. Here, that idea becomes the location of a human community whose stability has been violently disturbed.
